prayer.text: O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.

cues.text: A Girl Who Chose Mary for a Mother
Born in 1806 in the Burgundian village of Fain-lès-Moutiers, Catherine Labouré lost her own mother at nine years old.
She is remembered as having taken up a small statue of the Blessed Virgin at the funeral, kissed it, and declared, "now you will be my mother."
She entered the Daughters of Charity in Paris in 1830, beginning her novitiate that April at the community's motherhouse on the Rue du Bac .
Within months, she would receive the visions that changed the whole course of her quiet religious life.

Even as a small child, before any thought of religious life, Catherine had already shown an unusual seriousness in prayer, and her father's own attempts to discourage her vocation delayed, but never dimmed, her eventual entry into religious life.
The Virgin of the Chair
On the night of July 18, 1830, the eve of the feast of St. Vincent de Paul, Catherine reported being woken by a child's voice.
It called her to the chapel, where she found the Blessed Virgin seated in the director's chair, radiant with light.
Mary told her plainly, "God wishes to charge you with a mission.
You will be contradicted, but do not fear; you will have the grace to do what is necessary," and spoke as well of coming trials for France and for the Church.
This prophecy seemed confirmed within days, when revolution broke out in Paris on July 27.
The Virgin of the Globe
On November 27, 1830, during evening meditation, Catherine reported a second and more elaborate vision: Our Lady standing on a white globe.
Her feet were crushing a serpent, while her hands extended and streamed with rays of light representing the graces God wished to bestow on those who asked for them.
Around the figure appeared an oval frame bearing the words, in French, "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee," .
The vision then turned to reveal its reverse: a large M surmounted by a cross, with two hearts beneath, encircled by twelve stars.
Have a Medal Struck
Catherine understood herself instructed to have a medal made after this exact design, with the promise that all who wore it with confidence would receive great graces.

Her confessor, Fr. Jean-Marie Aladel , hesitated for a long time before acting, but eventually brought the matter before the Archbishop of Paris, who, after his own inquiry, permitted the medal to be struck in 1832.

What became known almost immediately as the Miraculous Medal spread with extraordinary speed across France and then the wider Catholic world, credited with numerous reported healings and conversions within its very first years.

Within a decade of the medal's minting, so many reported cures and conversions had been attributed to it that the ordinary faithful themselves had already begun calling it "miraculous" long before any formal Church document used the word.
A Hidden Life of Service
Catherine herself asked that her identity as the visionary be kept secret.
She spent the following forty-six years in humble, largely unnoticed service as portress and caretaker of the elderly and infirm at a hospice in Enghien, outside Paris.
Her extraordinary graces were known only to her confessor until shortly before her death.
Only in the final months of her life did she receive permission to reveal, briefly, what she had seen at Rue du Bac decades earlier.
Even the sisters who lived alongside her for decades had no idea that the humble portress in their midst had once knelt before the Mother of God.
She quietly told her own superior shortly before her death, revealing that this had occurred in that same convent's own chapel.
Legacy
An episcopal inquiry conducted by Archbishop Hyacinthe-Louis de Quélen found Catherine's account trustworthy and the Miraculous Medal genuinely inspired.
Devotion spread so widely and quickly that the medal is often credited with helping prepare the ground for Pope Pius IX's formal definition of the Immaculate Conception in 1854.
The medal's own inscription had, in effect, proclaimed that dogma a full generation in advance.
Catherine Labouré was canonized in 1947.
Nearly two centuries later, the Miraculous Medal remains one of the most widely worn sacramentals in the entire Catholic world.
It still carries the same simple prayer Our Lady asked a young, unremarkable novice to give to the whole Church.
